1.solution:
One \(\mathrm{O_2}\) molecule has mass \(32\) u, so \(100\) molecules have \(3200\) u.

\(1\ \mathrm{u} = 1.6605 \times 10^{-24}\) g, so \(3200\) u \(= 3200 \times 1.6605 \times 10^{-24} = 5.314 \times 10^{-21}\) g.

2.subtopic: Subatomic Particles, Isotopes, Isobars and Isoelectronic Species

3.subtopic: Group 16 Chalcogens, Oxygen, Sulphur and Ozone
3.solution: Down group 16 the central atom grows, the E-H bond becomes longer and weaker, and the hydride gives up hydrogen more easily. Reducing power rises from \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) to \(\mathrm{H_2Te}\), so \(\mathrm{H_2Te}\) is the strongest reducing agent.

4.solution: Iodine has 7 valence electrons: 5 bond pairs with F and 1 lone pair, 6 electron pairs in all (octahedral arrangement). With one position taken by the lone pair, the molecule is square pyramidal.

5.subtopic: Real Gases, Dalton's Law and KTG
5.solution: Kinetic theory gives the average kinetic energy per molecule as \(\dfrac{3}{2}kT\). It depends only on the absolute temperature, to which it is directly proportional, and not on pressure, volume or the kind of gas.

6.subtopic: Thermochemistry, Hess's Law and Bond Enthalpy
6.solution:
The three C-H bonds and one O-H bond appear on both sides and cancel.

Bonds broken: C-O \(+\) H-Cl \(= 335 + 431 = 766\) kJ. Bonds formed: C-Cl \(+\) H-O \(= 326 + 463 = 789\) kJ.

\(\Delta H = 766 - 789 = -23\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).

7.subtopic: First Law of Thermodynamics, Internal Energy and Work

8.solution: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. In an isothermal process the temperature does not change, so \(\Delta U = 0\).

9.solution:
\(\mathrm{CuCl_2}\) is a salt of a weak base and a strong acid: \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) hydrolyses and releases \(\mathrm{H^+}\), so its solution is acidic.

\(\mathrm{KNO_3}\) (strong acid, strong base) is neutral, \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\) is basic, and \(\mathrm{CH_3COONH_4}\) (weak acid, weak base of nearly equal strength) is close to neutral.

10.solution: \(\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}\) is the anion of a weak acid and hydrolyses: \(\mathrm{CO_3^{2-} + H_2O \rightleftharpoons HCO_3^- + OH^-}\). The \([\mathrm{OH^-}]\) rises and the solution is basic.

11.solution: \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\) is a salt of a weak base and a strong acid. The cation hydrolyses: \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2H_2O \rightleftharpoons Cu(OH)_2 + 2H^+}\), so the solution is acidic with pH below 7. It is the cation, not the anion, that reacts, and the solution turns blue litmus red.

12.subtopic: Group 1 Alkali Metals, Properties and Reactivity
12.solution: Alkali metals react with dihydrogen at high temperature to give ionic hydrides: \(\mathrm{2M + H_2 \rightarrow 2M^+H^-}\).

13.solution: Neopentane, \(\mathrm{C(CH_3)_4}\), is \(\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}\) like n-pentane and isopentane; the three differ only in how the carbon chain is branched. That is chain isomerism.

14.solution: The \(\mathrm{-OCH_3}\) group activates the ring and directs to ortho and para positions. The para product is major because the ortho positions are crowded by the methoxy group, so the main product is 4-nitroanisole (with 2-nitroanisole as the minor one).

15.solution: Benzene is both toxic and carcinogenic (it can cause leukaemia), which is why its use as a solvent is restricted.

16.subtopic: Unit Cells, Edge Length and Atomic Radius
16.solution: In fcc the atoms touch along the face diagonal: \(4r = \sqrt{2}a\), so \(r = \dfrac{a}{2\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{392}{2.828} = 138.6\) pm.

17.solution:
Anions at the 8 corners contribute \(8 \times \dfrac{1}{8} = 1\), and one cation sits at the body centre, so the cell holds one formula unit: \(Z = 1\).

\(\rho = \dfrac{ZM}{V N_A}\), so \(V = \dfrac{1 \times 168.6}{4 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}} = 7.0 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}\).

18.solution: A tetrahedral void is formed when one sphere sits over a hollow made by three spheres of the layer below. The four sphere centres lie at the corners of a tetrahedron, so 4 spheres surround the hole.

19.subtopic: Green Chemistry, Principles, Atom Economy and Green Solvents
19.solution: Dry cleaning traditionally used chlorinated solvents such as perchloroethylene, which are toxic and polluting. Liquid or supercritical \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) (with a suitable detergent) does the job without them, so it is the green alternative.

21.subtopic: Types of Solutions, Solubility and Henry's Law
21.solution: By Henry's law the solubility is proportional to the partial pressure: \(S = 6.85 \times 10^{-4} \times \dfrac{0.70}{1} = 4.795 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}\).

22.solution:
Both are non-electrolytes, so equal osmotic pressure at the same temperature needs equal molar concentrations.

\(6\) g/L urea \(= \dfrac{6}{60} = 0.1\) M and \(18\) g/L glucose \(= \dfrac{18}{180} = 0.1\) M. Only pair (A) matches.

23.subtopic: Molar Conductivity, Kohlrausch's Law and Degree of Dissociation

24.solution: In molten NaCl, \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) is oxidised at the anode, \(\mathrm{2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_2 + 2e^-}\), giving pale green chlorine gas. \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) is reduced at the cathode, \(\mathrm{Na^+ + e^- \rightarrow Na}\), giving liquid silvery sodium. Both (A) and (B) are correct, so (D) is the complete answer.

25.subtopic: Galvanic Cells, EMF, Nernst Equation and Thermodynamics
25.solution: A voltaic (galvanic) cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to produce electricity: chemical energy into electrical energy. Its anode is the negative electrode and its cathode the positive one, so (C) and (D) are wrong.

26.subtopic: Galvanic Cells, EMF, Nernst Equation and Thermodynamics
26.solution: The salt bridge connects the two half cells, completing the internal circuit, and lets ions flow to keep both solutions electrically neutral. It is not an electrode and does not measure anything.

27.subtopic: First-Order Kinetics, Rate Constant and Half-Life
27.solution:
After \(20\) min, \(40\%\) remains, a fraction \(0.4\). At \(84\%\) completion \(16\%\) remains, and \(0.16 = (0.4)^2\).

In a first order reaction equal times remove equal fractions, so reaching \((0.4)^2\) takes twice as long: \(40\) min.

28.subtopic: First-Order Kinetics, Rate Constant and Half-Life

29.subtopic: Rate Law, Order, Molecularity and Rate Expression
29.solution: For given concentrations the rate is proportional to the rate constant, so a larger rate constant means a faster reaction, not a slower one. (A), (B) and (C) are all true.

30.solution: Physisorption is exothermic and held by weak van der Waals forces, so by Le Chatelier's principle it decreases as the temperature rises. It increases with surface area and with stronger van der Waals forces.

31.solution: Interhalogens are covalent, volatile, non-explosive compounds that add to unsaturated hydrocarbons. They are strong oxidising agents (more reactive than the halogens themselves, except \(\mathrm{F_2}\)), not reducing agents.

32.subtopic: Colour, Magnetic Properties and Spin-Only Formula
32.solution:
An ion is paramagnetic if it has unpaired electrons. \(\mathrm{Ti^{2+}}\) is \(3d^2\), \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is \(3d^9\) and \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is \(3d^4\): all have unpaired electrons.

Each other set contains a diamagnetic ion: \(\mathrm{Ti^{4+}}\) (\(3d^0\)), \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) (\(3d^{10}\)) and \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) (\(3d^0\)).

33.solution: Zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^2\). It loses only the two 4s electrons; the completely filled 3d subshell is stable and does not take part, so zinc shows only the \(+2\) state.

34.subtopic: Bonding Theories, EAN, Crystal Field, Hybridization and Magnetism
34.solution: Fe(0) is \(3d^6 4s^2\). The strong-field CO ligands pair all the electrons into four 3d orbitals, leaving one 3d, the 4s and three 4p orbitals for the five CO lone pairs. That is \(dsp^3\) hybridisation, trigonal bipyramidal.

35.subtopic: Bonding Theories, EAN, Crystal Field, Hybridization and Magnetism
35.solution: The ligands donate lone pairs and the central metal ion accepts them, so the metal ion is a Lewis acid.

36.solution: The slow step of an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction is ionisation to a carbocation. A polar protic solvent stabilises the carbocation and the leaving anion by solvation, so it speeds the reaction. The nucleophile does not appear in the rate-determining step, so its strength does not matter.

37.subtopic: Preparation of Alkanes, Wurtz, Grignard and Decarboxylation
37.solution: Tertiary alkyl halides do not give the Wurtz coupling product: with sodium they mainly undergo elimination to the alkene. So the Wurtz reaction fails with tert-butyl chloride, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CCl}\).

38.solution:
Alcoholic KOH dehydrohalogenates 2-bromopropane to propene (A).

Without peroxide, HBr adds by Markownikoff's rule: H to the \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) end and Br to the middle carbon. B is 2-bromopropane.
38.note: the printed scheme is written here as a LaTeX reaction line; no figure needed

39.solution: In Williamson's synthesis the alkoxide attacks the alkyl halide by \(\mathrm{S_N2}\), so the halide must be primary. Sodium tert-butoxide with methyl bromide gives tert-butyl methyl ether. With tert-butyl bromide and methoxide (A), the strong base causes elimination to 2-methylpropene instead.

40.subtopic: Physical Properties of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
40.solution: Butane-1,3-diol has two OH groups and so forms extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds; it is also the heaviest of the four. Its boiling point is far higher than those of the bromoalkanes and of the single-OH compound (D).

41.solution: In the Cannizzaro reaction two molecules of an aldehyde without \(\alpha\)-hydrogen react with concentrated alkali: one is oxidised to the carboxylate and the other reduced to the alcohol. The same species is both oxidised and reduced, which is disproportionation.

42.solution: Acetaldehyde has a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO-}\) group, so it gives the iodoform reaction: \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO + 3I_2 + 4NaOH \rightarrow CHI_3 + HCOONa + 3NaI + 3H_2O}\). Besides yellow iodoform, it forms sodium formate.

43.subtopic: Preparation Methods of Aldehydes and Ketones
43.solution: \(\mathrm{R'MgX}\) adds to the C≡N of \(\mathrm{RCN}\) to give an imine salt, \(\mathrm{RR'C{=}NMgX}\). Acid hydrolysis converts it to the ketone \(\mathrm{RCOR'}\).

44.subtopic: Chemical Reactions and Basicity of Amines
44.solution: Only primary amines, heated with chloroform and alcoholic KOH, give the foul-smelling isocyanide: \(\mathrm{RNH_2 + CHCl_3 + 3KOH \rightarrow RNC + 3KCl + 3H_2O}\).

45.solution: Sodium and alcohol (Mendius reduction) add four hydrogen atoms across the C≡N: \(\mathrm{RC{\equiv}N + 4[H] \rightarrow RCH_2NH_2}\), a primary amine.

46.solution: Acetic anhydride acetylates every OH group. Glucose gives a pentaacetate, which shows it has five hydroxyl groups.

47.solution: The secondary structure (\(\alpha\)-helix and \(\beta\)-pleated sheet) is held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N-H groups of the peptide backbone.

48.solution: Terylene is the polyester of ethylene glycol (ethane-1,2-diol) and terephthalic acid (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid).

49.solution: Dacron is another name for terylene, poly(ethylene terephthalate).

50.subtopic: Carboxylic Acids, Properties, Reactions and Derivatives
50.solution: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) relieves pain and reduces fever: it is an analgesic (and antipyretic). It does not kill microbes.

51.solution:
(A) \(x = 1\) works. (B) \(x = 5\) works. (C) The smallest \(x\) is \(1\), and \(1 + 3 = 4 \ge 4\), so it holds for all.

(D) needs \(x < 1\), and no element of A is less than 1. So (D) is not true.

52.subtopic: Modulus and Argument — Polar Form, De Moivre and Square Roots
52.solution: \(-1 + \sqrt{-3} = -1 + i\sqrt{3}\), which lies in the second quadrant with \(r = 2\), \(\cos\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). So \(\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\).

53.subtopic: Arrangements with Constraints — Together, Never Together, Fixed Positions and Repeated Letters
53.solution:
Of the 8 places, the odd ones are 1, 3, 5 and 7. The 3 girls can take them in \({}^4P_3 = 24\) ways, and the 5 boys fill the remaining 5 places in \(5! = 120\) ways.

Total \(= 24 \times 120 = 2880\).

54.solution: \(\tan\) has period \(\pi\), so subtracting \(9\pi\) changes nothing: \(\tan(x - 9\pi) = \tan x\).

55.solution: \(\mathrm{cosec}\,\theta = -2\) means \(\sin\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}\). In \([0, 2\pi)\) the sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants: \(\theta = \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{7\pi}{6}\) and \(\theta = 2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\).

57.subtopic: General Second-Degree Equation — Condition for a Pair, Parallel Lines and Distances
57.solution:
Here \(a = 1\), \(b = -k\), \(h = 0\), \(g = -2\), \(f = 3\), \(c = -5\). The condition \(abc + 2fgh - af^2 - bg^2 - ch^2 = 0\) gives \(5k - 9 + 4k = 0\), so \(k = 1\).

The point of intersection satisfies both partial derivatives: \(2x - 4 = 0\) and \(-2ky + 6 = 0\), so \(x = 2\), \(y = 3\).

58.subtopic: Equation of a Circle — Centre-Radius, General, Diameter and Parametric Forms
58.solution:
The centre is equidistant from \((2, 3)\) and \((4, 5)\), so it lies on their perpendicular bisector: through \((3, 4)\) with slope \(-1\), that is \(x + y = 7\).

With \(y = 4x - 3\): \(5x - 3 = 7\), so the centre is \((2, 5)\). Radius\(^2\) \(= (2 - 2)^2 + (3 - 5)^2 = 4\).

\((x - 2)^2 + (y - 5)^2 = 4\) gives \(x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 10y + 25 = 0\).

59.subtopic: Limits — Existence, One-Sided Limits and Limits at Infinity
59.solution:
Right-hand limit: for \(3 < x < 4\), \([x] = 3\), so the expression is \(0\) and the limit is \(0\).

Left-hand limit: for \(2 < x < 3\), \([x] = 2\), so the expression is \(\dfrac{-1}{x - 3}\), which grows without bound as \(x \to 3^-\).

The one-sided limits differ, so the limit does not exist.

60.subtopic: Finding Truth Values of Component Statements
60.solution:
An implication is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent false. So \(\sim r\) is T (r is F), \(q \to r\) is T (so q is F), and \(p \vee q\) is T (so p is T). Check: \(p \wedge q\) is F, as needed.

With \(p = \mathrm{T}\), \(q = \mathrm{F}\): \(p \to q\) is F and \(q \to p\) is T.

61.subtopic: Logical Equivalence and Algebra of Statements
61.solution: \(a \to b \equiv \sim a \vee b\), so \((p \vee q) \to \sim r \equiv \sim(p \vee q) \vee \sim r \equiv (\sim p \wedge \sim q) \vee \sim r\) by De Morgan's law.

62.subtopic: Solution of Triangle — Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
62.solution:
\(A = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) and \(B = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\), so \(C = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

By the sine rule \(\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{3}/2} = 2\sqrt{3}\). Then \(b = 2\sqrt{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \sqrt{3}\) and \(c = 2\sqrt{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 2\sqrt{3}\).

63.subtopic: Inverse of a Matrix — Adjoint Formula, Products and Verification
63.solution:
\(A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos 120^\circ & -\sin 120^\circ \\ \sin 120^\circ & \cos 120^\circ \end{bmatrix}\), a rotation by \(120^\circ\). Then \(A^3\) is a rotation by \(360^\circ\), so \(A^3 = I\) and \(A^{-1} = A^2\).

So \(A^{-1} - A^2\) is the null matrix. A null matrix is diagonal and scalar (\(0 \cdot I\)), but it is not the unit matrix.

64.subtopic: Inverse of a Matrix — Adjoint Formula, Products and Verification
64.solution:
\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2i & -i \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(|A| = 2i - (-i)(-1) = i\) and \(\mathrm{adj}A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & i \\ 1 & 2i \end{bmatrix}\).

\(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{i}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & i \\ 1 & 2i \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -i & 1 \\ -i & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), using \(\dfrac{1}{i} = -i\).

65.subtopic: Inverse Trigonometric Functions — Principal Values and Evaluation
65.solution:
Let \(t = \sin^{-1}x\); then \(\cos^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - t\), and the expression is \(t^2 + \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - t\right)^2 = 2\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)^2 + \dfrac{\pi^2}{8}\).

Its minimum, at \(t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), is \(\dfrac{\pi^2}{8}\).

67.solution: Both square roots must be real: \(x - 1 \ge 0\) and \(3 - x \ge 0\), so \(1 \le x \le 3\). The domain is \([1, 3]\).

68.solution:
This is a \(1^\infty\) form: \(k = \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0}\left[\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4} + x\right)\right]^{1/x} = e^{L}\), with \(L = \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4} + x\right) - 1}{x}\).

L is the derivative of \(\tan\) at \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(\sec^2\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 2\). So \(k = e^2\).

The integral is \(-5\log|x - 3| + 6\log|x - 4| + c\).

79.solution:
\(2ax - x^2 = a^2 - (x - a)^2\), so \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2 - (x - a)^2}} = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x - a}{a}\right) + c\).

So \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}x\) and \(g(x) = \dfrac{x - a}{a}\).

82.solution: \(\left[x^2 + x\right]_1^a = a^2 + a - 2 = 5\), so \(a^2 + a - 7 = 0\). The sum of its roots is \(-1\).

83.subtopic: Area Between Two Curves — Intersections First
83.solution:
The curves \(y = \sin x\) and \(y = \cos x\) meet at \(x = \dfrac{9\pi}{4}\), where both equal \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). The shaded region lies under \(\sin x\) from \(2\pi\) to \(\dfrac{9\pi}{4}\) and under \(\cos x\) from \(\dfrac{9\pi}{4}\) to \(\dfrac{5\pi}{2}\):

\(\displaystyle\int_{2\pi}^{9\pi/4}\sin x\,dx + \int_{9\pi/4}^{5\pi/2}\cos x\,dx = \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 2 - \sqrt{2}\).

84.subtopic: Areas of Circles, Ellipses and Hyperbolas — Sectors, Segments and Standard Integrals
84.solution: The integral is the area of a quarter of the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 9\): \(\dfrac{1}{4}\pi(3)^2 = \dfrac{9\pi}{4}\).

85.solution:
\(\dfrac{dy}{y} = -\dfrac{2\,dx}{x}\) gives \(\log y = -2\log x + \log c\), that is \(x^2y = c\).

At \((2, 1)\): \(c = 4\), so \(x^2y = 4\), or \(x\sqrt{y} = 2\).

86.subtopic: Order, Degree, Formation of ODE, and Verification of Solutions
86.solution:
Divide by \(x\): \(\sin x + \dfrac{y^3}{x} = 4a\). Differentiating removes \(a\):

\(\cos x + \dfrac{3xy^2y' - y^3}{x^2} = 0\), so \(3xy^2y' = y^3 - x^2\cos x\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y^3 - x^2\cos x}{3xy^2}\).

87.subtopic: Order, Degree, Formation of ODE, and Verification of Solutions
87.solution:
Squaring removes the radicals: \(2 + \left(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^3 = \left(\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}\right)^5\).

The highest derivative is the third (order 3), and its power is 5 (degree 5).

89.subtopic: Vector Geometry — Section Formula, Triangle, and Parallelogram
89.solution:
\(\overline{AB} = -\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 4\hat{k}\), \(|AB| = 3\sqrt{2}\); \(\overline{AC} = -4\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 4\hat{k}\), \(|AC| = 6\).

The bisector of angle A divides BC in the ratio \(AB : AC = 3\sqrt{2} : 6 = 1 : \sqrt{2}\), so the point is \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}\,\bar{b} + \bar{c}}{1 + \sqrt{2}}\).

x: \(\dfrac{-\sqrt{2} - 4}{1 + \sqrt{2}} = (-\sqrt{2} - 4)(\sqrt{2} - 1) = 2 - 3\sqrt{2}\). y: \(\dfrac{6\sqrt{2} + 9}{1 + \sqrt{2}} = (6\sqrt{2} + 9)(\sqrt{2} - 1) = 3 + 3\sqrt{2}\). z: \(\dfrac{6\sqrt{2} + 6}{1 + \sqrt{2}} = 6\).

The point is \((2 - 3\sqrt{2})\hat{i} + (3 + 3\sqrt{2})\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\).

90.subtopic: Scalar Triple Product, Coplanarity, and Volume
90.solution:
Coplanar vectors have a zero scalar triple product:

\(\begin{vmatrix} a & a & c \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ c & c & b \end{vmatrix} = a(0 - c) - a(b - c) + c(c - 0) = c^2 - ab = 0\).

So \(c = \sqrt{ab}\), the geometric mean of \(a\) and \(b\).

104.solution:
\(\vec{v} = \dfrac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = -a\omega\sin\omega t\,\hat{i} + a\omega\cos\omega t\,\hat{j}\).

\(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{v} = -a^2\omega\sin\omega t\cos\omega t + a^2\omega\sin\omega t\cos\omega t = 0\), so the angle is \(90^\circ\) (uniform circular motion).

105.subtopic: Elasticity, Springs, and Energy in Strained Solids
105.solution: In series the same force F stretches each spring: \(x_1 = \dfrac{F}{K_1}\), \(x_2 = \dfrac{F}{K_2}\). Total extension \(= F\left(\dfrac{1}{K_1} + \dfrac{1}{K_2}\right)\).

107.subtopic: Rotational Kinetic Energy and Rolling Motion

108.subtopic: Variation of g with Depth, Altitude, Density, and Latitude
108.solution:
g is greatest at the surface, so it decreases both above and below it: Statement I is correct.

For small heights \(g_h = g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)\) while \(g_d = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)\). These are equal when \(d = 2h\), not when \(d = h\): Statement II is incorrect.

109.subtopic: Viscosity, Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Reynolds
109.solution: Terminal velocity \(v = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}\) is proportional to the square of the radius, so the big drop falls at \(V\dfrac{R^2}{r^2}\).

110.subtopic: Viscosity, Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Reynolds
110.solution:
At terminal velocity the viscous force balances weight minus buoyancy:

\(F = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3(\rho - \sigma)g = \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times (10^{-3})^3 \times 9000 \times 9.8 = 3.696 \times 10^{-4}\) N \(= 3696 \times 10^{-7}\) N.

So \(x = 7\).

111.note: the printed figure (a beaker of oil over mercury with the sphere across the boundary) only illustrates the stem, which says everything it shows; kept text-only

112.solution:
Thermal resistance is \(\dfrac{l}{kA}\). With \(R_0 = \dfrac{l}{KA}\), the rods have resistances \(\dfrac{R_0}{2}\), \(R_0\), \(\dfrac{R_0}{2}\): total \(2R_0\).

Heat current \(H = \dfrac{3T - T}{2R_0} = \dfrac{T}{R_0}\).

\(T_1 = 3T - H\dfrac{R_0}{2} = \dfrac{5T}{2}\) and \(T_2 = T_1 - HR_0 = \dfrac{3T}{2}\), so \(\dfrac{T_1}{T_2} = \dfrac{5}{3}\).

113.subtopic: Radiation — Stefan, Wien, Newton's Law of Cooling, Black Body
113.solution: The radiating surface is the curved surface of the wire, \(\pi dL\). By Stefan's law \(P = e\sigma(\pi dL)T^4\), so \(e = \dfrac{P}{\sigma T^4\pi dL}\).

114.subtopic: Radiation — Stefan, Wien, Newton's Law of Cooling, Black Body
114.solution:
By Wien's law \(\lambda_m T\) is constant, so the new temperature is \(\dfrac{2}{3}T\).

Power \(\propto T^4\): \(\dfrac{P'}{P} = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^4 = \dfrac{16}{81}\).

115.subtopic: First Law, Internal Energy, and Work-Heat Relations
115.solution: The work in a cycle equals the area enclosed on the p-V diagram. ABCD is a rectangle \(2V_0\) wide (from \(3V_0\) to \(5V_0\)) and \(2P_0\) high (from \(2P_0\) to \(4P_0\)), so the magnitude of the work is \(4P_0V_0\). (The cycle runs anticlockwise, so the net work done by the gas is negative.)

116.subtopic: Isothermal, Adiabatic, Isobaric, and Isochoric Processes
116.solution: Isothermal: \(P_A = 2P\). Adiabatic: \(P_B = P \times 2^\gamma\), and \(\gamma > 1\), so \(P_B > 2P\). Hence \(P_A < P_B\).

117.subtopic: Gas Laws and Ideal Gas Equation
117.solution:
At fixed volume, \(PV = \dfrac{m}{M}RT\) gives \(m \propto \dfrac{P}{T}\).

\(\dfrac{m_2}{6} = \dfrac{(P/2)/300}{P/500} = \dfrac{500}{600}\), so \(m_2 = 5\) g. The hydrogen that leaked out is \(1\) gram.

118.subtopic: SHM Kinematics — Displacement, Velocity, Phase, and Damping
118.solution:
\(x = A\sin\omega t\). From 0 to \(\dfrac{A}{2}\), the phase goes from 0 to \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\): that is \(\dfrac{T}{12} = 2\) s, so \(T = 24\) s.

From \(\dfrac{A}{2}\) to A the phase goes from \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) to \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(\dfrac{T}{6} = 4\) s.

119.subtopic: SHM Energy — Kinetic, Potential, and Total
119.solution: The total energy of SHM is \(E = \dfrac{1}{2}Ka^2\). It is the same at every displacement, so it depends only on K and a.

120.subtopic: Sound Wave Properties, Speed, and Intensity
120.solution: Water vapour is lighter than dry air, so moist air is less dense. Since \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma P}{\rho}}\), the speed of sound increases with humidity.

121.solution: The string's frequency is \(n + x\) or \(n - x\). More tension raises the string's frequency. If that reduces the beats, the string was moving towards n from below, so its frequency was \(n - x\).

122.subtopic: Progressive Wave, Wave Equation, and Velocity
122.solution:
\(\mu = \dfrac{10^{-3}}{0.5} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\) kg/m, so \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.8}{2 \times 10^{-3}}} = 20\) m/s.

A pulse is inverted at each fixed end. After reflecting from the far end and then from the near end it is upright again, having travelled \(2L = 1\) m in \(\dfrac{1}{20} = 0.05\) s. A new pulse produced at that moment coincides with it and adds constructively, so \(\Delta t_{min} = 0.05\) s.

123.solution: Work done moving a charge is \(q\,\Delta V\), and on an equipotential surface \(\Delta V = 0\), so the work is zero. Statement a is not true; b, c and d are true.

124.solution:
In contact both spheres reach the same potential, \(\dfrac{kq_1}{R} = \dfrac{kq_2}{3R}\), so \(q \propto r\).

\(\sigma = \dfrac{q}{4\pi r^2} \propto \dfrac{1}{r}\), hence \(\dfrac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_2} = \dfrac{3R}{R} = 3\).

125.solution:
The forces on q from Q and from 4q must cancel: \(\dfrac{kqQ}{a^2} + \dfrac{kq(4q)}{b^2} = 0\), so \(Q = -4q\dfrac{a^2}{b^2}\), where a and b are the distances of Q and 4q from q.

With 4q at the end of the line (\(a = \dfrac{d}{3}\), \(b = d\)): \(Q = -\dfrac{4q}{9}\), option (D).

As printed, with 4q at \(\dfrac{2d}{3}\): \(Q = -4q \times \dfrac{1}{4} = -q\), which is not among the options.
125.note: as printed (4q at 2d/3) the answer is Q = -q, which is not an option; option D, -4q/9, is the answer when 4q sits at distance d (the end of the line). Kept PRIVATE.

126.solution:
The field magnitude is the slope of the V-x graph, \(|E| = \left|\dfrac{dV}{dx}\right|\).

In regions 1 and 3, V is constant, so \(E_1 = E_3 = 0\). In region 4, V falls more steeply than it rises in region 2, so \(E_2 < E_4\).

127.solution: With a slab of thickness t: \(C = \dfrac{\epsilon_0 A}{d - t + \frac{t}{K}} = \dfrac{\epsilon_0 \times 40 \times 10^{-4}}{(2 - 1 + 0.2) \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{4}{1.2}\epsilon_0 = \dfrac{10}{3}\epsilon_0\) F.

128.solution:
First balance: \(\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{l}{100 - l}\), so \(l = 40\) cm.

The shunt lowers the right-hand resistance, so the balance moves to \(62.5\) cm: \(\dfrac{2}{R'} = \dfrac{62.5}{37.5}\), giving \(R' = 1.2\,\Omega\).

\(\dfrac{3X}{3 + X} = 1.2\) gives \(1.8X = 3.6\), so \(X = 2\,\Omega\).

130.subtopic: Classification, Curie's Law, Hysteresis, and Shielding
130.solution:
A diamagnetic substance has a small negative susceptibility that does not depend on temperature. Its graph is a horizontal line below the T-axis: graph C.

(Graph B, \(\chi \propto \dfrac{1}{T}\), is Curie's law for a paramagnetic substance.)

131.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
131.subtopic: Magnetic Moment of Current Loop and Galvanometer Instruments
131.solution:
With N turns, \(L = N \cdot 2\pi r\), so \(r = \dfrac{L}{2\pi N}\) and \(NA = N\pi r^2 = \dfrac{L^2}{4\pi N}\).

The maximum torque is \(NiAB = \dfrac{iBL^2}{4\pi N}\), largest when \(N = 1\).

132.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
132.solution:
P is at distance r from each wire with \(2r^2 = 7^2\), so \(r = \dfrac{7}{\sqrt{2}} = 5\) cm \(= 0.05\) m.

Each field is perpendicular to its own line to P, and those lines are perpendicular, so the two fields are perpendicular:

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi r}\sqrt{8^2 + 15^2} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 17}{0.05} = 68 \times 10^{-6}\) T.

133.solution:
Side \(= 5\) cm \(= 0.05\) m, pulled out in 1 s, so \(v = 0.05\) m/s.

\(e = Blv = 40 \times 0.05 \times 0.05 = 0.1\) V, and the power dissipated is \(\dfrac{e^2}{R} = \dfrac{0.01}{10} = 10^{-3}\) W.

Over 1 s the work done is \(1.0 \times 10^{-3}\) J.

134.solution:
Moving at v, the edge of width l in the field gives \(e = Blv\) and current \(I = \dfrac{Blv}{R}\). The magnetic force on that edge is \(BIl = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}\), opposing the motion.

No acceleration means this force balances the weight: \(\dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R} = mg\), so \(v = \dfrac{mgR}{B^2l^2}\).

135.subtopic: Self-Inductance, Energy Stored, and LR Circuit
135.solution: The branches \(R\)-\(B_1\) and \(L\)-\(B_2\) are in parallel, and the switch is in the common line to the battery. When S is opened the battery is cut off, but the inductor opposes the fall of its current: the current keeps flowing round the closed loop made by the two branches, through both bulbs. The same decaying current passes through \(B_1\) and \(B_2\), so both go off with the same delay.

138.solution:
\(X_L = \omega L = 2000 \times 5 \times 10^{-3} = 10\,\Omega\) and \(X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{2000 \times 50 \times 10^{-6}} = 10\,\Omega\): the circuit is at resonance.

The total resistance is \(6 + 4 = 10\,\Omega\) (the coil's own resistance counts), so \(I_0 = \dfrac{30}{10} = 3\) A.

139.solution: For a telescope \(M = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\), so a large magnifying power needs an objective of large focal length (and an eyepiece of small focal length).

140.solution: At Brewster's angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other: the angle between them is \(90^\circ\).

145.subtopic: de Broglie Wavelength and Matter Waves
145.solution:
Photon: \(\lambda_p = \dfrac{hc}{E}\). Electron: \(\lambda_e = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mE}}\).

\(\dfrac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p} = \dfrac{E}{c\sqrt{2mE}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{E}}{c\sqrt{2m}}\), which is proportional to \(\sqrt{E}\), that is \(\sqrt{E} : 1\).

146.solution: The Coulomb force supplies the centripetal force: \(\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{ke^2}{r^2}\), so \(KE = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{ke^2}{2r}\), proportional to \(\dfrac{e^2}{2r}\).

147.solution:
In the first orbit \(mvr = \dfrac{h}{2\pi}\), so \(v = \dfrac{h}{2\pi mr}\).

Revolutions per second \(= \dfrac{v}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{h}{4\pi^2mr^2}\).

148.solution:
\(G_1\) and \(G_2\) are NOT gates giving \(\bar{A}\) and \(\bar{B}\). \(G_3\) is a NOR gate: \(\overline{\bar{A} + \bar{B}}\). \(G_4\) inverts it again: \(Y = \bar{A} + \bar{B} = \overline{A \cdot B}\).

That is a NAND gate.

149.subtopic: Transistors — BJT, CE Amplifier, and Gain

150.subtopic: Band Theory, Doping, and Semiconductor Types
150.solution: In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor the charge carriers come only from covalent bonds broken by thermal energy, which creates equal numbers of electrons and holes. Doped (extrinsic, p- or n-type) semiconductors get most of their carriers from impurities.
